justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an equity index or ETF priced around 256. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 256.1 is essentially a near-flat projection, reflecting the well-documented finding that short-term price changes are difficult to predict and that the best naive forecast is something very close to the current price. The slight upward tilt comes from the historical positive drift embedded in equity markets over time, even when compressed to a single session. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate to 257.5, incorporating that same drift assumption over five trading days while remaining cautious about mean-reversion tendencies. At the one-month horizon, 260.0 reflects a continuation of the trend, roughly consistent with annualized equity returns of around 7–10% when scaled down to a monthly window.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, and this is intentional. At one day, realized volatility for a broad equity instrument in the 250 range typically implies a daily move of roughly 1–2%, which maps to a roughly ±5-point range at the 90% level. At one week, uncertainty compounds — not just because daily volatility accumulates roughly as the square root of time, but also because macro data releases, central bank communications, and geopolitical developments can emerge within any five-day window. By one month, the interval widens to ±24 points around the point estimate, reflecting the full range of macro and market-specific forces that can materially reprice assets over a 20-trading-day period.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in economic data — such as a sharp miss in employment figures or a surprise in inflation — could trigger a risk-off move that breaks below the lower bound. A sudden escalation in geopolitical tensions or a credit event in a systemically important institution would similarly be capable of producing outsized drawdowns. On the upside, a surprisingly dovish pivot from a major central bank, a blowout earnings season, or a resolution of a major macro overhang could accelerate the rally beyond 284 at the one-month horizon. These tail events are precisely why the intervals are set at 90% rather than 99% — roughly one in ten outcomes should fall outside them under normal distributional assumptions.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly stationary volatility conditions. In practice, volatility itself is stochastic and can spike dramatically in short windows — think VIX doubling in a single session during a crisis.
